[1] The following page provides a reference to resources that may guide countries in adapting the guidelines for use in the country.
[2] The fourth level (L4: Executable: reference applications and services) focuses on the software applications and services within a digital ecosystem. Its purpose is to include executable reference software that accurately represents the intentions and the operational and functional requirements of WHO recommendations; responds to the needs of users and of the health system; and comprises machine-readable data and calculations within interoperability standards, as documented in levels L1–L3. As a fully functional application, its purpose is to serve as a generic starting point, ready to be adapted locally to the specific operational context of the users, the population and the health system in which it is deployed. Other products at this level include terminology services to support consistent data representation for interoperability purposes; reusable software libraries, including software development kits; application programming interfaces; and functions as a service to support updates of content and FHIR capabilities across all subscribed digital systems.
[3] The standards-based technical artifacts of this implementation guide sit at the third level of knowledge representation (L3: Machine-readable recommendations). It provides the code necessary for software developers to incorporate into digital systems the standardized logic of the WHO guidelines, which can be subjected to conformance testing against the standards, including fidelity to the recommendations. A standards-based technical implementation guide builds on the operational level (L2) by mapping the L2 content to value sets and to the Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources (FHIR) standards of Health Level Seven International. Together with the L2 data standards, this enables semantic and syntactic interoperability at scale. The logic derived from the guidelines, which could include clinical decision support and performance indicator calculations, can be encoded in Clinical Quality Language (CQL). This ensures that key indicators can be extracted consistently to support patient care, as well as case surveillance and programme monitoring. The machine-readable representations of this implementation guide are intended to be adapted to countries' digital health service delivery and reporting systems. Digital solutions that include L3 machine-readable recommendations can then be subjected to conformance testing against the interoperability standards.
[4] This implementation guide provides the generic content needed in digital systems, independent of any particular software application and with the intention that countries can adapt it to meet local needs.
[5] To apply WHO recommendations in country settings, governments must interpret and then adapt the content in accordance with local policies, procedures and digital tools.
[6] WHO guidelines formulate and support rigorously evaluated recommendations on health interventions intended to be adopted in country programmes. To ensure that countries can effectively benefit from investments in digital health, the SMART Guidelines approach aims to facilitate the accurate reflection of WHO clinical, public health and data use guidelines in the digital systems that countries are adopting.
